raw_case_text:
A 45-year-oldfemale presented to IMS and SUM Hospital, Bhubaneswar, with gradually progressing symptoms of yellowish discoloration of sclera, reduced appetite, pain abdomen with vomiting, and weight loss for 2 months. On examination, she was conscious and oriented with marked icterus and no pallor. The abdomen was soft on palpation and elucidated tenderness, particularly in the right hypochondrium. The liver function tests were deranged with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, bilirubin in urine, and raised prothrombin time. She was a rural resident, illiterate, nonobese, nondiabetic person. She had no family history of any malignancy. She did not have any history of smoking and alcoholism and no history of enteric fever in the recent past. Her bile culture was sterile, and she was seronegative for HIV, hepatitis C virus, and hepatitis B virus. Her routine single stool examination was negative for any parasite. Ultrasonography (USG) of the abdomen showed a lobulated outline of gallbladder (GB) neck and body and growth with contiguous hepatic infiltration forming a mass. There was infiltration of primary biliary confluence with moderate bilobar intrahepatic biliary radical (IHBR) dilatation and infiltrated second part of the duodenum as well as multiple metastatic lesions in the liver. Contrast computed tomography (CT) showed hepatosplenomegaly with IHBR dilatation with abrupt tapering in the middle part of the common bile duct (CBD). The gallbladder was over distended with three irregular soft-tissue densities around 4.1 cm x 2.6 cm in the lumen. Thus, a preliminary diagnosis of inoperable Stage IV carcinoma gallbladder metastasizing to the liver was put forth. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) was planned for biliary cannulation with stenting as a palliative measure. Astonishingly, multiple adult worms were visualized in the duodenum on ERCP [Figure 1], two of which could be recovered during the procedure while the other two escaped into the large intestine. The isolated parasites were large approximating 25-30 mm x 12-15 mm, flat, brownish, and leaf like [Figure 2]. Each worm's posterior end was pointed, and the oral sucker was situated in the conical projection at the extreme anterior end of the organism. Thus, it was morphologically identified as Fasciola hepatica. We did not find any eggs in her stool or those of the closely associated family members on careful direct examination and by concentration technique.
Since the patient had an inoperable tumor, she received palliative therapy for advanced stage of gallbladder carcinoma. She received antihelminthic drug albendazole for parasite clearance following which she was discharged on request.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 45-year-old female presented in Bhubaneswar, India, with a 2-month history of progressive scleral jaundice, anorexia, right upper quadrant abdominal pain, vomiting, and weight loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the preceding 2 months, the patient experienced gradually progressive yellowish discoloration of the sclerae, reduced appetite, abdominal pain accompanied by vomiting, and unintentional weight loss.
subjective.past_medical_history: Rural resident, non-obese, non-diabetic; no recent history of enteric (typhoid) fever, no family history of malignancy, and no history of tobacco smoking or alcohol use.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for progressive jaundice, anorexia, abdominal pain, vomiting, and weight loss.

objective.physical_examination: On admission, the patient was conscious and oriented with marked scleral icterus and no pallor. Abdominal examination revealed a soft abdomen with localized tenderness in the right hypochondrium.
objective.routine_investigations: Liver function tests demonstrated conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, bilirubinuria, and prolonged prothrombin time. Viral serologies for HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C were negative, bile culture was sterile, and routine direct and concentrated stool examinations (of the patient and family members) were negative for ova and parasites. Abdominal ultrasonography showed an overdistended gallbladder with a lobulated mass in the gallbladder neck and body directly infiltrating the contiguous liver parenchyma and second part of the duodenum, primary biliary confluence involvement with moderate bilobar intrahepatic biliary radicle dilatation, and multiple hepatic metastases.
objective.advanced_workup: Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT confirmed hepatosplenomegaly, an overdistended gallbladder containing three irregular intraluminal soft-tissue masses (~4.1 cm x 2.6 cm), hepatic metastases, and bilobar intrahepatic biliary dilatation with abrupt mid-common bile duct tapering (Stage IV gallbladder carcinoma). During palliative endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) for biliary stenting, multiple live, flat, leaf-like brownish adult trematode worms (measuring 25-30 mm x 12-15 mm with a pointed posterior end and an anterior conical projection bearing an oral sucker) were visualized in the duodenum; two adult worms were endoscopically extracted and morphologically identified as Fasciola hepatica.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Inoperable Stage IV gallbladder carcinoma with hepatic metastases and malignant biliary obstruction co-existing with incidental duodenal Fasciola hepatica infestation, confirmed by hepatobiliary ultrasound/contrast CT and direct endoscopic extraction and morphological identification of adult Fasciola hepatica flukes during ERCP. Enteric fever and viral hepatitis were absent. The patient was treated with oral albendazole for parasite clearance and palliative care for advanced gallbladder malignancy, and was subsequently discharged at her request.
